description: Shared ideas: an idea taught in more than one place. A skill idea is a way of thinking each subject uses in its own way (evidence and claims); a topic idea is content taught in more than one place (the water cycle). Each member gives a role: first (where students first meet it), builds_on (goes deeper), applies (uses it in its own context) or repeats (teaches it again at about the same level, often the same year: the overlaps worth coordinating). Membership is recorded only here. See HOW-IT-WORKS.md, 'Cross-subject links'. Called 'threads' until 11 Nov 2026; renamed because the framework uses 'thread' for the strands inside one unit.
source: Learning Waypoints prior-knowledge node pass, 10 Nov 2026. Skill-thread frames for evidence and claims are from the node pass; the rest, the topic threads and all roles were drafted from the members' node labels and checkpoints (10 Nov 2026).

shared_ideas.title: Evidence and claims
shared_ideas.description: Telling a claim from evidence for it: fact or opinion, who says so and how they know, how far the evidence goes, and whether several independent lines support it. The biggest overlap across subjects; fact versus opinion alone is taught in four places.
shared_ideas.outside_kit: The ACARA Digital Literacy general capability (investigating information) teaches it too; Kit has no node files for general capabilities.

members.frame: History: is it a factual claim or an opinion? Check it against other sources; accuracy versus usefulness.
History: who made the source, when and why.
History: fact versus interpretation; building an argument from evidence.
English: fact or feeling? The language of opinion versus factual reporting.
English: back up a judgement with evidence from the text and other sources.
English: a paragraph that makes a claim and backs it with an example, evidence and explanation.
English: evaluate how a text uses sources and quotations.
Economics: what the data shows, a reasonable inference, or a claim that goes too far.
Civics: burden of proof and evidence in court.
Science inquiry: check a claim for hidden assumptions and evidence that disagrees.
Science: several independent lines of evidence support plate tectonics.
Science: several independent lines of evidence support evolution.
Science: several independent lines of evidence support the big bang theory.
Maths statistics: critique statistical arguments in the media.
Maths statistics: critique statistical reports in the media.

shared_ideas.title: Perspective and bias
shared_ideas.description: Whose view a source or text gives, and how that view shapes what it says.

members.frame: English: identify bias in the language of a text.
Civics: identify perspectives in civic sources and explain why they differ.
History: the perspective in a historical source, the values behind it, and who is missing.

shared_ideas.title: Idea structures
shared_ideas.description: Common ways of organising ideas: sorting into groups and subgroups, cause and effect, time order, problem and solution, compare and contrast. English names the structures; other subjects use them.

members.frame: English: name the ways texts organise ideas: groups and subgroups (taxonomies), cause and effect, and time order (chronology).
English: add problem and solution, and compare and contrast.
Science: sort living things into groups and subgroups (a taxonomy).
History: putting events in time order (chronology), and their causes and effects.
Economics: cause-and-effect relationships in economic data.
Economics: respond to an issue by weighing costs and benefits (problem and solution).
Geography: strategies for water sustainability (problem and solution).

shared_ideas.title: Inquiry questions
shared_ideas.description: Asking a question you can actually answer by testing or researching. The four humanities subjects share one framing; science asks for investigable questions separately.

members.frame: HASS Year 6: develop questions that guide every stage of an inquiry.
Civics: develop a civic inquiry question, often from current events.
Economics: what makes a question one you can research, using economics ideas.
Geography: ask a geographical question rather than a general one, and plan how to investigate it.
History: what makes a question historical, and its scope.
Science: questions you can answer by testing (investigable) versus ones you can't.

shared_ideas.title: Searching and organising information
shared_ideas.description: Finding sources with a search strategy, choosing what's relevant, and organising it, including choosing a table or graph.
shared_ideas.outside_kit: The ACARA Digital Literacy general capability teaches search and choosing a chart too; Kit has no node files for general capabilities.

members.frame: HASS Year 6: choose ways to collect information, judge sources, and organise it.
Civics: locate information with search strategies, then select and organise it.
Economics: search with a clear aim, pick what's relevant, and organise data in a suitable format.
Geography: find secondary materials and represent data in geographical formats.
History: find sources in archives and collections with search strategies, then sort them for the inquiry.
Maths: tables and graphs, and what they show about how data is spread.
Maths: choose the right table or graph for the data and the purpose.

shared_ideas.title: Classification
shared_ideas.description: Sorting things into groups by their features: useful, with trade-offs, and open to change. All three members are in Year 7.

members.frame: Science: why we sort living things into groups, using yes/no keys (dichotomous keys), and how the groups change over time.
Geography: classify resources as renewable, non-renewable or continuous.
Maths: step-by-step yes/no rules (algorithms) that sort shapes.

shared_ideas.title: Logic: and, or, not
shared_ideas.description: The same three logical operations, taught in two subjects in the same year.

members.frame: Digital Technologies: logic gates (circuits that do AND, OR, NOT) and why computers use binary.
Maths: "and", "or" and "not" for combined events in probability.

shared_ideas.title: Water cycle
shared_ideas.description: Evaporation, condensation and precipitation moving water around Earth. Taught in Year 4 science, then met again twice in Year 7.

members.frame: Science: evaporation, condensation and precipitation as one continuous cycle.
Science: explains evaporation and condensation with the particle model.
Science: evaporation used to separate a mixture.
Geography: how moving water connects places, re-teaching the cycle in the same year as science.

shared_ideas.title: Weathering, erosion and deposition
shared_ideas.description: Rock broken down, moved and laid down somewhere else. Science and Geography each teach it, Geography twice.

members.frame: Science: weathering breaks rock down; erosion, transport and deposition move it.
Geography: moving water as a force that changes the landscape.
History: stratigraphy, layers laid down in order, used to date finds.
Geography: weathering, erosion, transport and deposition again, as landform processes.
Science: deposited layers turn into sedimentary rock (lithification).

shared_ideas.title: Dating and deep time
shared_ideas.description: How we know how old things are, and how long Earth's history is. History uses radiocarbon dating two years before science explains half-life.

members.frame: History: radiocarbon dating and other evidence for early human migration.
History: dating techniques again, among the scientific methods historians use.
Science: geological time, over millions of years.
Science: half-life, the science behind radiocarbon dating.

shared_ideas.title: Human evolution
shared_ideas.description: Where humans came from. History meets the theories in Year 7; science explains the mechanism in Year 10.

members.frame: History: theories of human evolution and the evidence for them.
Science: natural selection as the mechanism, with several lines of evidence.

shared_ideas.title: Rates
shared_ideas.description: One quantity per unit of another. Maths teaches it in Year 8, but science uses it in Year 7 (density).

members.frame: Science: density, mass per unit of volume, a year before maths teaches rates.
Maths: rates as comparisons of different units, in practical problems.
Digital Technologies: speeds in hardware specifications (GHz, Mbps).
Digital Technologies: bandwidth, data per second.
Digital Technologies: sampling rate, samples per second.
Science: acceleration, change in velocity per second.
Science: reaction rate.

shared_ideas.title: Line graphs over time
shared_ideas.description: Reading how something changes over time on a line graph. Maths teaches it in Year 5; six standards in other subjects use it.

members.frame: Maths: read and interpret line graphs, including change over time.
Maths: relationships shown in graphs of real data.
Science: population changes in a food web.
Science: a heating curve.
Geography: rainfall over time on climate graphs.
Economics: trends in economic data.
Civics: trends in Australia's diversity data.
Science: indicators of climate change.

shared_ideas.title: Percentages
shared_ideas.description: A percentage of a quantity. Maths teaches it in Years 6 to 8; most other subjects use it.

members.frame: Maths: find a percentage of a quantity.
Maths: calculations with percentages.
Maths: percentage increase and decrease in real contexts.
Science: about 10% of energy passes to the next level of a food web.
Civics: percentages of the population in diversity data.
Economics: budgeting.
Science: efficiency as a percentage.
Digital Technologies: how much compression saves.

shared_ideas.title: Plate tectonics and landforms
shared_ideas.description: Forces inside Earth that build landforms and cause hazards. Science and Geography both teach it in Year 8.

members.frame: Science: Earth's layers, plates and what happens at their boundaries.
Geography: endogenic processes (forces from inside Earth) that build landforms, in the same year as science.
Geography: volcanoes and earthquakes as hazards for people.

shared_ideas.title: Climate and environmental change
shared_ideas.description: How human activity changes environments, and what to do about it. Science and Geography both teach it in Year 10.

members.frame: Science: how greenhouse gases change Earth's energy balance, the evidence, and responses.
Geography: types of human-induced environmental change, in the same year as science.
Geography: causes of an environmental change and strategies to manage it.
